blocks.prompt: The Dragonfly That Never Misses
blocks.text: A dragonfly does not start out in the air. It starts under the water. A baby dragonfly is called a nymph. It has no wings yet. It walks around on the mud at the bottom of the pond. It hunts tiny bugs down there. It stays under the water for a long time. Some stay for years. Then one day the nymph climbs up a plant stem into the air. Its back splits open. Out comes a dragonfly with four new wings. It dries them in the sun. Then it flies away.

3.title: The Dragonfly That Never Misses

blocks.prompt: How a Dragonfly Hunts
blocks.text: A dragonfly's head is almost all eye. Each of its two big eyes is built from thousands of tiny lenses, packed together like the cells of a honeycomb. Together they let the dragonfly see nearly all the way around itself without turning its head. It can watch you and watch its dinner at the same time. Its four wings are just as unusual. Most insects flap both pairs of wings together. A dragonfly can move each wing on its own. That is why it can hover in one spot, slide sideways, and even fly backward. Put those two things together and you get a hunter that almost never misses. A dragonfly does not chase a bug from behind. It watches where the bug is going and flies to the empty air where the bug will be. When scientists filmed dragonflies hunting, the dragonflies caught their target about nine times out of ten. Most hunters on Earth miss far more often than that.

blocks.prompt: The Years Before the Wings
blocks.text: The dragonfly you see skimming over a pond in July has already lived most of its life, and it lived that life underwater, out of sight. It began as an egg laid in or near the water. What hatched was not a small dragonfly. It was a nymph: brown, wingless, and built like a tank. The nymph crawls through mud and dead leaves at the bottom of the pond, and it is a serious predator. It carries a folded lower lip under its face, hinged like a grabbing arm. When a tadpole or a mosquito larva drifts past, the nymph shoots that lip out, hooks the prey, and pulls it back to its jaws. The whole strike takes a fraction of a second. The nymph breathes through gills tucked inside the end of its body. If it needs to escape, it squeezes water out through the same opening and rockets forward like a jet. This stage is not short. Depending on the species and the water, a nymph may spend one year down there, or two, or as many as five. It molts again and again, splitting out of a shell that has grown too tight. Then, on a chosen night, the nymph climbs a reed and leaves the water for the first time. Its skin splits along the back. The adult drags itself out, pumps fluid into four crumpled wings until they stretch flat and clear, and waits for them to harden. By morning it can fly. It has weeks, maybe a couple of months, to live in the air. The empty nymph shell stays clamped to the reed behind it.

5.title: The Dragonfly That Never Misses
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Globe skimmer: Pantala flavescens
The longest known migration of any insect

The round trip may cover 11,000 miles
No single dragonfly finishes the loop

blocks.prompt: The Insect That Crosses an Ocean
blocks.text: There is a dragonfly, about the length of your thumb, that crosses an ocean. It is called the globe skimmer, and it is probably the most widespread dragonfly on Earth. Every year, globe skimmers leave southern India and fly out over open water toward East Africa. There is nothing to land on. There is no food, no fresh water, no shelter. The crossing is roughly two thousand miles of nothing but sea, and the round trip, made by a chain of generations, may cover eleven thousand miles. No other insect is known to travel so far. They do not do it by muscle alone. Globe skimmers ride the monsoon. They climb into moving air, sometimes more than half a mile up, and let the wind carry them while they hold a long, cheap glide. A dragonfly's wings can be locked out flat, turning the insect into a sailplane, and its four wings are driven by muscles attached directly to the wing bases, which is unusual and gives it fine control at low cost. The timing is the clever part. The monsoon rains that push them along also fill the desert with temporary pools, and a temporary pool is exactly what a dragonfly needs. Nymphs hatch, hunt, and grow fast in warm shallow water. By the time the pool dries, a new generation is in the air, following the rain to the next place it will fall. No individual completes the loop. Each one flies its leg of the journey and lays eggs, and the species keeps going without any single dragonfly knowing the whole route. Scientists worked this out slowly, by matching arrival dates to wind maps, by finding globe skimmers on ships and on islands with no fresh water at all, and by testing the chemistry of their wings, which carries a signature of the water they grew up in. The evidence points the same way from every direction: a two-inch insect, with no map and no chance to practice, is riding a weather system across an ocean, and has been doing it for a very long time.

6.title: The Dragonfly That Never Misses
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Odonata, in the air for about 300 million years
Meganeura: a Carboniferous relative with a two-foot wingspan
Up to 30,000 lenses per compound eye
Some species carry around 30 opsins; humans carry 3
Capture rate about 95 percent in lab tests
Sixteen paired nerve cells steer the intercept

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Flying Machine
blocks.text: Dragonflies were flying before there were flowers, before there were birds, before there were dinosaurs. The order they belong to, Odonata, and its close extinct relatives were already in the air roughly 300 million years ago, and the basic design has not needed much revision since. That is worth sitting with. Almost every flying thing you have ever watched is a newcomer by comparison. The ancient ones were larger. In the Carboniferous swamps, a griffinfly called Meganeura carried wings that spanned about two feet, roughly the wingspan of a pigeon. It was not a true dragonfly, but it was built on the same plan. The usual explanation for its size is oxygen. Insects have no lungs. They breathe through a branching network of tubes called tracheae that carry air directly to the tissues, and that system works only over short distances. Carboniferous air held far more oxygen than today's air does, so the tubes could reach deeper and the body could afford to be bigger. When oxygen levels fell, the giants went with them. What survived is the pocket-sized version, and the pocket-sized version is arguably the better machine. Consider the eyes. A dragonfly's head is mostly eye: two compound domes assembled from as many as thirty thousand separate lenses, each aimed in a slightly different direction, giving the animal a field of view that is nearly complete. Human color vision runs on three types of light-sensitive protein. Some dragonflies carry more than twenty, and a few species carry around thirty, tuned across a range that includes ultraviolet light we cannot see at all. It is not that a dragonfly sees a sharper world than you do. Its resolution is poor by our standards. It sees a faster one. Its eyes refresh so quickly that a movie would look to it like a slideshow of still pictures. Consider the wings. Four of them, each hinged separately, each driven by muscles that pull on the wing base directly rather than by squeezing the whole chest the way a bee's flight muscles do. That arrangement lets a dragonfly beat its front and back wings out of phase for efficient hovering, in phase for a burst of speed, or hold them still and glide. It can hover, reverse, climb, and turn inside its own length. Nothing else in the air, including anything we have built, does all of that in one body. Then there is the hunting, which is where the eyes and the wings become a single argument. When a dragonfly attacks, it does not follow its prey. Following is a losing strategy, because a chaser is always behind. Instead the dragonfly holds the target at a fixed angle in its visual field and flies to the point where the target is going to be, adjusting continuously so that the prey appears not to move against the background. Fighter pilots use the same geometry and call it a constant bearing. A set of sixteen paired nerve cells runs from the dragonfly's brain to its wing muscles, carrying the correction. In laboratory tests, dragonflies hunting fruit flies caught them about ninety-five percent of the time. A lion, hunting hard, misses far more often than it succeeds. So this is the summary: an animal older than birds, running an interception problem on a brain smaller than a grain of rice, with a hit rate no predator with a spine can match. And most of that life happens somewhere you never look. The adult you see over the water in August has already spent one to five years as a wingless nymph in the mud below it, hunting with a hinged lip that fires out like a spring-loaded arm. The flying part, the part that gets our attention, is the short final chapter. It lasts a few weeks. Then a new nymph is already down there in the dark, waiting out its own long apprenticeship, running the same 300-million-year-old design.
